title: Distributed outage simulation - traffic orchestration & regional capacity review

Customer to provide traffic profile CSV and current autoscaler settings
Schedule 2-hour chaos test window week of 2025-11-03
SE to run a short latency vs batching benchmark on customer's 8-bit quantized model
action_items: Maya: send DR runbook and links to playbook doc by 2025-10-20
Arjun: produce baseline throughput/latency spreadsheet and sample curl commands by 2025-10-22

summary: Redwood SEs walked Luminary through a focused technical deep dive on multi-region routing, capacity planning, and an executable DR simulation plan. Discussed policy-driven traffic shaping (latency vs cost), KV cache warmup strategies, batching/quantization tradeoffs for production latency SLOs, VPC tunneling concerns for private deployment, and a proposed chaos/evacuation simulation to validate failover runbooks.
topics: policy routing (latency-priority, cost-priority, sticky sessions), regional capacity sizing, DR simulation and evacuation playbook, KV cache priming and consistency, batching & quantization impacts on P95/P99, private deployment networking (VPC peering, IP allowlists), monitoring and tracing for failover verification
transcript:
00:00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're on for an hour, but we left a bit of buffer. Quick roll call?
00:00:06 Jared Klein: Jared here, Priya, Elena, Marcus, Olivia on my side.
00:00:09 Maya Chen: Awesome. I'll hand to Arjun to frame the technical agenda.
00:00:13 Arjun Patel: Thanks. Today we want to walk through how routing policies can be used to meet your latency SLOs during region failures, how regional capacity is sized, and then run through a proposed DR simulation — basically an evacuation test. Also we'll touch on KV cache priming and what happens to prefix cache on failover.
00:00:30 Priya Rao: Quick ask — we need the plan to include on-prem hops, we will have an air-gapped site for some PHI workloads.
00:00:36 Arjun Patel: Noted. We'll cover VPC/on-prem routing.
00:00:40 Sofia Martinez: Also we'll call out expected RTO/RPO for the different failure classes.
00:00:45 Jared Klein: Sounds good. Our primary concern is that P95 latency stays under 480ms for patient-facing APIs. Cost is secondary but still important.
00:00:54 Arjun Patel: Okay, that's helpful. We'll show a few routing profiles: latency-first, cost-first, and sticky-session (session affinity) for stateful KV-heavy flows.
00:01:05 Elena Bhat: And security-wise, we need to confirm audit logs and KMS behavior during failover — keys shouldn't leak and audit continuity is needed.
00:01:13 Diego Ramos: We'll include notes on key management, we often recommend KMS in each region with cross-region key access disabled for the most restrictive setup.
00:01:21 Marcus Yoon: Practical Q — when you fail traffic from us-east to us-west, how do you warm the KV caches to avoid a cold spike? That's where we saw big tail latency in our tests.
00:01:33 Arjun Patel: Great question. Two approaches: async pre-warming using recorded prefix traces, or on-demand bulk warmup during a controlled cutover. Pre-warm is safer but needs the trace; on-demand will elect a brief higher latency window while the new region builds prefix/KV entries.
00:01:49 Priya Rao: We have 30 days of logs but not in a nice prefix-format. Is there tooling?
00:01:54 Arjun Patel: We'll share a small script that converts request logs into a top-k prefix list — it's in the playbook.
00:01:59 Maya Chen: I'll attach that after the call.
00:02:02 Priya Rao: Great.
00:02:05 Arjun Patel: On batching and quantization: we saw you mentioned 8-bit quantization in your notes. For short prompt lengths with tight latency SLOs, 8-bit with lower batching (batch size 4-8) often gives best P95 tradeoff. For throughput-heavy background jobs, 4-bit quant can be more cost-efficient but sometimes increases variance in tail.
00:02:26 Olivia Park: So would you recommend different quant profiles per route?
00:02:30 Arjun Patel: Exactly. The routing policy can map to model variants — e.g., latency-route -> model-8bit-low-batch, cost-route -> model-4bit-high-batch. The runtime supports auto-fallback if a variant is unavailable.
00:02:44 Jared Klein: If there's an auto-fallback, does the API surface indicate the variant used so we can tag traces?
00:02:49 Sofia Martinez: Yes, we can inject headers and tracing tags with model_variant, region, node_id. That helps in comparing postmortems.
00:02:57 Elena Bhat: About compliance — does the audit log persist across region failover so we don't lose chain-of-custody?
00:03:02 Diego Ramos: Audit logs are stored in the control plane and can be replicated. For Private deployments with a customer-managed control plane, we recommend log shipping to the customer's SIEM with an append-only setup.
00:03:12 Priya Rao: Network constraints — our egress to certain regions is throttled. That could block peering.
00:03:18 Arjun Patel: Then we should design a routing profile that prefers regional warm standby inside the same cloud provider and same region family, and only cross-cloud as last resort.
00:03:27 Marcus Yoon: Let's walk through a sample evacuation scenario.
00:03:30 Arjun Patel: Sure. Scenario 1: us-east-1 partial outage — control plane healthy, worker VMs down. Policy: initiate 'regional evacuation' which does: 1) Pause new session pinning, 2) Route new requests to us-west-2 with latency-policy, 3) Initiate cache warm-up in us-west-2 from top-k prefixes, 4) Increase batch window for background jobs to free capacity, 5) Trigger alerting & status updates. Expected RTO ~ 90s to start routing, P95 stabilizes in ~8-10 minutes after warmup if pre-warm not used.
00:04:09 Jared Klein: 8-10 minutes is a lot for patient UI. Is there any way to reduce that?
00:04:14 Arjun Patel: Two levers: maintain a small hot-warm pool in each region (extra reserved capacity), or run continuous micro-warmers that keep the most common prefixes warm. Both cost more.
00:04:26 Priya Rao: What about sticky sessions? Some of our workflows rely on ephemeral context in the cache.
00:04:31 Arjun Patel: If you rely on KV cache locality for session continuity, we'd recommend session affinity with sticky-routing and a replication TTL strategy on KV entries. Alternatively, persist critical session state to your app DB so it is re-hydrated on failover.
00:04:46 Olivia Park: Re: KV replication — does Redwood replicate KV cache between regions?
00:04:50 Arjun Patel: We don't actively cross-replicate KV cache across regions by default because it's expensive and consistency is hard. We do offer an optional asynchronous snapshot/replication for select prefixes for customers that need it; it's eventual.
00:05:03 Priya Rao: So during failover we'd expect some cache misses and heavier compute.
00:05:07 Arjun Patel: Correct. That's why warmup is important.
00:05:10 Sofia Martinez: On observability side, we recommend synthetic canaries that validate both correctness and latency — a canary that exercises a representative prompt set every 30s.
00:05:19 Marcus Yoon: We'll need playbook steps for rollback if warmup causes overload.
00:05:24 Arjun Patel: Playbook includes: rollback to original region routing, throttle new sessions, scale up dedicated capacity if reserved pools exist, and engage manual drain of in-flight long requests.
00:05:34 Elena Bhat: Can you show the sample routing policy DSL?
00:05:38 Arjun Patel: Sure — (reads) policy { priority: latency, fallback: cost, regions: [primary, warm-standby], affinity: session, kvcache_warmup: top_k(1000) async } — it's simplified. You can tune thresholds and timeouts.
00:05:56 Olivia Park: Does the runtime respect sequence-length-based kernel selection across variants? We saw different P95 depending on kernels.
00:06:03 Arjun Patel: Yes — we have kernel selection that adapts to token length distributions; quantized kernels may choose different matmul kernels. That's why we recommend sampling production token lengths and testing variants with those distributions.
00:06:15 Priya Rao: About VPC/on-prem — we plan to keep some inference inside our VPC for PHI. How does private deployment routing work?
00:06:24 Diego Ramos: You can run Redwood Private with a control plane managed by Redwood or self-hosted; inference nodes live in your VPC. For cross-region failover, traffic can be routed to another private deployment region via peered VPCs or a secure tunnel. We support static allowlists and mTLS for the control plane.
00:06:41 Priya Rao: Does the control plane need to be reachable if the primary region's control plane is down?
00:06:46 Diego Ramos: If you self-host the control plane in multiple regions you can survive control plane region failure; otherwise we have fallbacks. For strict isolation, we recommend dual-control-plane topology.
00:06:56 Jared Klein: Quick nit — what's the impact on billing when routing across regions?
00:07:00 Arjun Patel: Cross-region routing can incur egress and replication costs; also different GPU types have different per-token costs. That's why a cost-priority fallback is useful.
00:07:09 Elena Bhat: On key management again — if KMS is regional and the primary key is unavailable, what's the behavior?
00:07:14 Diego Ramos: If you use regional KMS keys with no cross-region access, the node in the failing region can't decrypt. So either pre-provision keys or use a key-wrapping approach where an encrypted secret can be decrypted in the target region. We document the tradeoffs.
00:07:30 Priya Rao: Can we get an example of a chaos test?
00:07:33 Arjun Patel: Yes. Proposed chaos test outline: 1) baseline collect 30 minutes of metrics; 2) simulate worker node loss in primary region; 3) observe routing transition and KV miss rate; 4) run a synthetic traffic spike; 5) validate P95/P99 and correctness; 6) run rollback and verify metrics return to baseline. We'll provide scripts for points 2,3,4.
00:07:54 Marcus Yoon: If the synthetic spike is severe, will Redwood autoscale quickly enough?
00:07:59 Arjun Patel: Autoscaling is tuned to produce additional pods in ~60-120s depending on cloud provider and instance availability; dedicated reserved capacity allows faster scale because nodes are warmed.
00:08:11 Priya Rao: So reserved capacity reduces RTO. How much reserved should we buy?
00:08:15 Arjun Patel: A common approach: cover your 95th percentile regional peak with reserved capacity and let burst capacity handle short spikes; then route traffic under failure to the union of reserved capacity across remaining regions. We'll size based on your submitted traffic CSV.
00:08:30 Olivia Park: About tracing tags again — can we tie model_variant to our APM?
00:08:34 Sofia Martinez: Yes, we provide trace instrumentation for common APMs and you can map tags to spans.
00:08:39 Jared Klein: Any special considerations for long-running streaming requests during failover?
00:08:44 Arjun Patel: Streaming will be interrupted when a node fails; we recommend a client-side reconnection strategy that will request the missing suffix and we can include a continuation token. For strict at-most-once semantics, persist progress at the app layer.
00:08:57 Priya Rao: Let's talk about metrics we should monitor during the test.
00:09:00 Sofia Martinez: Key metrics: region-specific P95/P99 latency, KV miss rate, cold-start rate, batch size distribution, CPU/GPU utilization by node, queue lengths, and model_variant fallbacks. Also synthetic canary pass rate.
00:09:13 Marcus Yoon: For alerting thresholds: what would you suggest for P95?
00:09:17 Sofia Martinez: If your SLO is 480ms P95, alert at 550ms, page at 700ms, and critical at sustained 1-minute P95 > 900ms. Those are examples.
00:09:30 Elena Bhat: For SOC2 evidence, we need a documented simulation and outcome. Will Redwood provide a runnable report?
00:09:36 Maya Chen: Yes, we'll give a simulation report template that you can consume.
00:09:40 Jared Klein: Anything else on quantization specifics?
00:09:43 Arjun Patel: One more note: 4-bit quantization sometimes requires different kernel selection which can increase P99 variance; for patient-facing APIs I'd cautiously use 8-bit or mixed quant profiles.
00:09:55 Priya Rao: Noted.
00:09:58 Arjun Patel: Ok, let's demo a mini-run through of a policy change in the console. Nina?
00:10:03 Nina Li: I'll share my screen — sorry for the momentary delay.
00:10:10 Nina Li: (screen) Here's the policy editor — you can see we can chain conditions: if region healthy == false then route to fallback set, set model_variant = latency-8bit, kvcache_warmup = async(top_k=500), affinity = false, throttle_new_sessions = true. You can set timeouts and escalation hooks.
00:10:31 Olivia Park: Can that be versioned? We need auditability.
00:10:34 Nina Li: Yes, policies are versioned, and we keep diffs in the config audit.
00:10:39 Jared Klein: How do we test a policy without impacting prod?
00:10:41 Nina Li: We have a 'canary' toggle to apply policy to 0.5% of traffic, or a dry-run mode that simulates decisions and logs them.
00:10:50 Priya Rao: Show me the dry-run logs.
00:10:53 Nina Li: (scrolling) Here — you'll see decisions recorded along with reason codes and hypothetical fallbacks.
00:11:02 Marcus Yoon: Back to KV cache: if we opt for async snapshot replication of top prefixes, what's the RPO?
00:11:09 Arjun Patel: It's eventual; typical lag is 30s-2min depending on size and bandwidth. It's not a strict RPO guarantee.
00:11:18 Priya Rao: Wouldn't that still help shrink warmup time?
00:11:21 Arjun Patel: Yes, it is usually effective — if you can tolerate eventual consistency for non-critical prefixes.
00:11:25 Jared Klein: Let's record the key decisions for the DR plan.
00:11:29 Maya Chen: Decision 1: Run a controlled evacuation test week of 2025-11-03 with Redwood scripting. Decision 2: Customer will provide traffic CSV and 95th/99th percentiles. Decision 3: Try a hybrid quant profile: 8-bit for patient UI, 4-bit for batch jobs.
00:11:45 Priya Rao: Decision 4: For PHI, maintain private deployment with dual control planes in two regions.
00:11:51 Elena Bhat: Decision 5: Use asynchronous KV replication for top-1k prefixes for faster warmup.
00:11:57 Maya Chen: Great. Any other open questions?
00:12:00 Jared Klein: On pricing, can we get an estimate of cross-region egress impact for a 20% failover?
00:12:05 Diego Ramos: We'll model that in the pricing sheet.
00:12:09 Arjun Patel: One last technical gotcha — client retries: if clients retry aggressively during failover, they can amplify load. Put an exponential backoff and client-side jitter.
00:12:19 Olivia Park: We'll check our SDKs.
00:12:22 Maya Chen: Okay I'll recap and then we'll open the floor for more specific SOC and network questions. Recap in chat.
00:12:29 [--- FAST-FORWARD SUMMARY V/O BY FIRELIES AUTO-SUMMARY ---]
00:12:35 System: Summary — routing policies for latency vs cost, KV cache warmup strategies, quant/batching tradeoffs, private deployment networking, and a proposed chaos test with clear action items.
00:12:50 Jared Klein: Thanks. A few network-specific things — our internal firewall blocks 443 egress to some AWS regions; is that a blocker?
00:12:57 Diego Ramos: If egress is blocked, you'd need a peered VPC in an allowed region or a proxy that can route to the permitted region. We'll document options.
00:13:06 Priya Rao: Also, can we get a list of required ports and IPs for test windows?
00:13:10 Maya Chen: Yes — we'll send a spreadsheet with endpoints and ports.
00:13:14 Marcus Yoon: Let's talk about how to validate correctness of model outputs post-failover.
00:13:18 Arjun Patel: We'll run diff checks against a representative eval set and watch for regressions; Redwood Optimize can run lightweight evals during the test and alert on metric drift.
00:13:28 Olivia Park: That would be great.
00:13:30 Priya Rao: Any special notes about on-prem hardware? We use a mix of T4s and A10s.
00:13:36 Arjun Patel: Kernel selection and quant perf differ across GPUs. We'll recommend per-instance benchmark runs. On T4 you may see higher latency per token than A10. We'll include a sample benchmark harness.
00:13:48 Jared Klein: Ok folks, let's wrap — thanks for being thorough.
00:13:51 Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with artifacts and schedule the chaos window.
00:13:55 Elena Bhat: Thanks.
00:13:57 [call ends]
